head:
Adults · Strength

Grip strength, a health indicator

Squeezing a device for a few seconds seems trivial. Yet studies have had hundreds of thousands of people do it, then counted who was still alive, who could still walk unaided, who had fallen ill. This article does not assume the test is useful: it puts it to the test, from the most general level to the most specific, then tells you what you can do with it.

The question

You squeeze a dynamometer, a handheld device with a gauge, and you read a number in kilograms. That number is used in research that has followed very large groups of people for years. Teams have linked it to lifespan, heart disease and the independence of older people. The idea is quickly reduced to a slogan: “your grip predicts your lifespan”.

This idea appeals because it is simple, but it calls for two precautions. A measure that goes along with a risk is not what causes it: a rising thermometer does not cause the fever. And most of these studies involve middle-aged or older adults, whereas you may be 25 or 35.

The question

Does your grip strength, measured once in a few seconds, say anything reliable about your future health? And if so, what can you do with it, at your age, so that this number is useful for something other than worrying?

We ask it because both wrong answers have a cost. Ignoring the test means missing a benchmark that costs a few seconds. Over-interpreting it means worrying about a number that does not say what it is made to say, or building up your forearm in the belief that it will lengthen your life.

What is at stake

What is at stake is not gym performance. Four things depend on your muscular strength, and therefore on what this test is supposed to reflect.

Your independence. Getting up from a chair, walking at a brisk pace, dressing yourself: these movements require strength, and you only notice it when it is missing.

Your health and your lifespan. Large cohorts link grip to deaths from cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease and cancer. If this link holds, a test lasting a few seconds is an almost free screening tool. If it does not hold, it should be used neither to reassure nor to alarm.

Your starting capital. Strength builds up until around thirty, holds for a few years, then erodes. What you build now determines where you start from for the descent.

Your training. If you train, you want to know whether this number measures something useful or a detail of the hand, because the answer changes what you work on.

These stakes cannot be left unanswered: the test already exists and everyone will interpret it anyway. It is better to do so with the evidence in hand. Here is the path.

  1. What grip measures. A proxy, not the hand itself.
  2. What a normal grip looks like. A life-course curve, with wide gaps.
  3. The link with lifespan. Across hundreds of thousands of people.
  4. The link with independence, at any age. Beyond mortality.
  5. The objections. Age, illness, leg strength, causality.
  6. What can change, and what remains uncertain. Training, young adults.
rest:
Step 1 of 6What grip measures, and what it is supposed to reveal

Starting claim: grip strength is a proxy for your overall muscular strength, not a measure of your hand.

Grip strength is the maximum force you can exert by squeezing your hand. It engages the muscles of the hand and forearm, and depends on the nervous system that controls them. It was adopted in medicine for a practical reason: it can be measured in a few seconds, with an inexpensive device, in almost everyone.

The underlying reason is a hypothesis: a weak hand often signals a lack of strength throughout the body, and muscular strength is what protects against frailty. The European consensus on sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle, places low muscular strength at the centre of its definition.1

What this means

You are not measuring your hand: you are measuring a proxy. The rest of the article consists of checking whether this proxy is a good one, that is, whether it foretells something, whether it is reliable, and whether it can be acted on.

Before making it say anything about health, you need to know what an ordinary grip looks like. That is the next step.

Step 2 of 6A normal grip is not a number: it is a life-course curve, with wide gaps

Claim: before judging your grip, you need to place it according to your age and sex, and accept that the gaps between people are wide.

British researchers pooled nearly 50,000 people aged 4 to 90 from 12 population studies to chart grip by age.2 The chart shows the medians and, around them, the zone where 80% of people fall.

Your grip rises until around thirty, holds, then declines, with wide gaps between people of the same age

Men, medianWomen, medianShaded zone: 80% of people of that age and sex

Grip strength (kg) by age. Lines: medians (half do better, half do worse). Zones: 10th to 90th percentile. Cross-sectional data (different age groups measured at the same time). Source: Dodds et al., PLoS ONE, 2014, table 2.2

Read it in three stages. First the shape: grip rises until early adulthood, holds through the forties, then declines. The peak of the median is 51 kg in men (between 29 and 39 years) and 31 kg in women (between 26 and 42 years). The authors place the start of the decline as early as the forties.2 Then the level: men are stronger than women at every adult age, which makes it pointless to compare yourself with the other sex. Finally the width of the zone: at 40, 10% of men squeeze less than 38 kg and 10% more than 63 kg; among women of the same age, less than 23 kg and more than 39 kg.

Cross-reading the table makes age more telling: the median 80-year-old man (32 kg) squeezes less hard than the weakest 10% of men aged 40 (under 38 kg). Among women, 19 kg at 80 against 23 kg. The study does not make this comparison; it is our own calculation.

The authors also define a “weak” grip: at least 2.5 standard deviations below the peak of young adults, i.e. about 27 kg in men and 16 kg in women. At 80, 23% of men and 27% of women fall below this threshold.2 This threshold was designed to identify frail older people, not to judge someone in their thirties.

What this means

Your strength is not a constant: it builds up, it holds, then it goes down, and the descent speeds up with age. What you build before 40 is a starting capital; what you maintain afterwards slows the loss. And a number is only worth something compared with people of your age and sex: 38 kg is weak for a 40-year-old man, ordinary for a 75-year-old man. Limitation: the curve compares different groups at the same moment, and its authors specify that it should not be used to track one person's trajectory.2

We now know what a normal grip is. The real question becomes: does being below normal for your age foretell anything? We first look at the largest possible number of people.

Step 3 of 6In very large cohorts, a weaker grip goes with a higher risk of death

Claim: at equal age and sex, people with a weaker grip die more often in the following years.

The broadest evidence comes from the international PURE study. It measured grip in 139,691 adults aged 35 to 70 in 17 countries with very different incomes, then counted deaths over a median of 4 years: about 2% of participants, or 3,379 people.34 For each 5 kg less of grip, the risk of all-cause death is 16% higher. For cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular deaths, 17% higher in both cases. The authors accounted for, among other things, diet, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, BMI, blood pressure and a history of stroke or cancer.4

Sixteen per cent seems small. Two clarifications help in reading it. The figure is relative: if 2 people in 100 died within 4 years, a risk 16% higher corresponds to about 2.3 in 100 (simplified calculation, derived from these two figures). And the increments add up, as the chart shows.

Each 5 kg less of grip adds a step to the risk

All-cause death risk index, with the reference set at 100. The bar at 116 comes from the study (risk ratio of 1.16 per 5 kg less). The two hatched bars are calculated here (1.16 squared, then cubed), assuming the effect repeats identically at each increment: this is an extrapolation, not a measured result. Source: Lancet, PURE study, 2015.3

What this means

A grip clearly below that of your age group goes, on average, with a higher risk of death, and the gap grows with the shortfall. The PURE authors find that grip predicts all-cause and cardiovascular death better than systolic blood pressure, measured in the same study.4 This does not prove that squeezing harder prolongs life: grip behaves like a barometer, which falls when the body is more fragile.

A single result is not enough. Three other sources point the same way.

The UK Biobank cohort followed 502,293 adults aged 40 to 69 for 7.1 years on average, with 13,322 deaths. For each 5 kg less, the risk of all-cause death is 20% higher in women and 16% in men; of cardiovascular death, 19% and 22%; of respiratory death, 31% and 24%; of death from cancer, 17% and 10%.5 In Korea, the KLoSA cohort (5,859 people aged 50 and over, 515 deaths) compares the weakest third (20.25 kg or less) with the strongest third (29.0 kg or more): risk of death multiplied by 1.90, risk of cardiovascular death by 1.59, and no clear link for cancer.8 Finally, a meta-analysis of 14 studies (53,476 people) finds a risk multiplied by 1.67 for the weakest quarter compared with the strongest quarter, with large differences from one study to another, and a link also visible in five studies whose mean age is under 60.7

These four sets cover varied continents and incomes, and point in the same direction. This is a strong argument for a real association. It does not yet say anything about the cause.

Dying earlier is not the only outcome that matters. If grip is a true proxy for strength, it should also foretell how we live, not just for how long. And if the link exists, it should not wait for old age.

Step 4 of 6The link is not limited to mortality: it affects independence, and it starts early

Claim: grip measured in adulthood goes with the ability to walk, get up and look after oneself decades later, and its link with health is already present in adolescents.

The Honolulu Heart Program measured grip in 6,089 men aged 45 to 68 (54 on average), with no known disease at baseline. It saw them again 25 years later, between ages 71 and 93, to test their walking, their ability to get up from a chair and their everyday tasks.9

The men who had the weakest grip at 54 walk more slowly and get up with more difficulty 25 years later

Strongest third (reference)Middle thirdWeakest third

Adjusted odds ratio, strongest third = 1.0. An odds ratio of 2.87 means odds 2.87 times higher, which is not a risk multiplied by 2.87. Third limits: 37.0 and 42.0 kg. 6,089 men of Japanese origin from Hawaii, with no known disease at baseline, followed for 25.3 years; 3,218 took the final examination. Source: Rantanen et al., JAMA, 1999.9

What this means

The men whose grip at 54 was in the weakest third (under about 37 kg) had odds almost three times higher of walking at 0.4 m/s or less, which is very slow, and of being unable to get up from a chair without using the arms. The odds of difficulty dressing, washing, eating or going to the toilet were more than doubled in the weakest third (for example 2.69 for dressing).9 Grip therefore informs us not only about death, but about the quality of the last decades, and the link can be read over more than twenty years.

And in young people? The Swedish cohort (1,142,599 adolescents aged 16 to 19, followed for a median of 24 years, 26,145 deaths) measured strength in adolescence. The strongest, on grip or leg strength, had a 20 to 35% lower risk of premature death, from all causes or cardiovascular causes, after accounting for BMI and blood pressure. In the weakest tenth, mortality was 122.3 per 100,000 person-years, against 86.9 in the strongest: about 30% lower (gap calculated here). No link with cancers appears; however, the strongest had a 20 to 30% lower risk of suicide.10 The authors speak of an emerging risk factor, of a weight comparable to that of BMI or blood pressure.10

Two caveats so as not to flatter the picture. In UK Biobank, several links are slightly stronger in the youngest.56 But in PURE, grip was not significantly associated with hospitalisations for diabetes, COPD or pneumonia, nor with falls and fractures.4 It therefore does not foretell everything: its link is clearest for deaths and functional decline.

So far, everything is consistent: the same direction everywhere, at both ends of life. This is precisely the moment to be wary. A neat convergence can have an ordinary explanation. The next step looks for the flaw.

Step 5 of 6The objections: age, illness, leg strength, causality

Claim: the link survives the main objections, but it is more modest and more indirect than the headlines say.

Objection 1: it is just age

Older people have both a weaker grip and a higher risk of death. Part of the link could be nothing more than that. The American NHANES study (10,470 adults) gives the results before and after adjustment.11

A large part of the raw gap comes from age, but a substantial gap remains once age is accounted for

MenWomen

Risk ratio of all-cause death, weakest fifth of grip versus strongest fifth (1.0 = same risk). 10,470 American adults (NHANES), 847 deaths, 81 months of mean follow-up. Source: Xiong et al., Frontiers in Nutrition, 2023.11

What this means

The objection is largely valid for the raw gap: it drops from about 14 to 3.4 in men as soon as the effect of age and BMI is removed. But it does not disappear: people in the weakest fifth for their age still have a risk of death about three times higher than those in the strongest fifth, even when smoking, alcohol and known diseases are taken into account. Only the adjusted figures count, such as those of PURE and UK Biobank.

Objection 2: it is illness that weakens the hand

This is reverse causality. A person who is already ill loses strength and is more likely to die: grip would then be a consequence of illness, not a signal that precedes it. The Honolulu study excluded at baseline men with diabetes, arthritis, stroke, heart attack or angina, and measured grip twenty-five years before the independence assessment. The link persists, and decreases only modestly when diseases that appeared in the meantime are added (2.87 becomes 2.77 for slow walking).9 The Swedish study measures strength at 16-19, an age when serious chronic diseases are rare (general reasoning, not a result of the study). On the other hand, the NHANES article read here does not report an analysis excluding the first years of follow-up.11 Reverse causality therefore probably explains part of the link in older people, and explains poorly that in adolescents.

Objection 3: grip does not represent all of your strength

The starting reasoning was: a weak hand signals general weakness. A European team tested it by comparing grip with thigh strength (knee extension) in 960 people from 5 cohorts.12

Grip and leg strength go in the same direction, but far less closely than is assumed

Correlation between grip and knee extension strength, by group; the bar covers the published values for both sexes. 960 people, 5 cohorts. A correlation of 0.45 corresponds to about one fifth of shared variation (0.45 squared: derived calculation). Source: Yeung et al., JAMDA, 2018.12

What this means

The two strengths go together, but are very far from a perfect link: a correlation of around 0.4 to 0.5 means that about one fifth of the variation in one is explained by the other (derived calculation). In practical terms, someone can have a good grip and weak legs, or the reverse. The authors conclude that grip alone should not be taken for overall strength.12 For you: the test is one indicator among others, and that is an argument for pairing it with a leg measurement.

Objection 4: predicting is not explaining, and does not always predict very well

In UK Biobank, adding grip to a classic risk score (age, sex, diabetes, BMI, blood pressure, smoking) improves the prediction of deaths only modestly: the C-index gains 0.013 for all-cause mortality. The authors call for further work before making it a screening tool.56 The two results are reconcilable: grip alone predicts better than blood pressure alone in PURE, but it adds only a little when the two are combined.

That leaves causality itself. One clue comes from genetics: using genetic variants linked to grip (16 regions of the genome identified in 195,180 people), researchers find a probable causal effect of higher strength on a lower risk of fracture.13 It concerns genetically predicted strength, not what you would gain by training, and it is in tension with PURE, which found no link between grip and fractures.4 The point remains open.

What the objections leave standing: a robust association, an imperfect proxy, an unproven cause. That leaves the practical question, the one that concerns you: can this proxy be changed, and do we know whether we gain anything by doing so?

Step 6 of 6What can change, and what remains uncertain

Claim: grip can be trained, overall strength seems to matter, but no one has shown that improving the number lengthens life, and the question of a decline in young adults is open.

Grip can be trained

A meta-analysis of 24 trials (3,018 healthy adults aged 60 and over, 73 on average) finds that exercise increases grip significantly but by a small amount (standardised effect of 0.28). Varied training, or training centred on specific movements, seems the most effective.14 In sarcopenic older people, another meta-analysis (13 trials, 711 people) concludes that resistance training improves grip, with reservations: few studies, very different protocols.15 We did not find any trial in healthy young adults.

Overall strength seems to matter

A meta-analysis of 16 cohorts of adults links strength training to a 10 to 17% lower risk of death, cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes, with a maximal effect at around 30 to 60 minutes per week.16 The WHO recommends that adults do muscle-strengthening activities involving the major muscle groups on at least two days per week.17 Be careful about what these figures say: they concern strength training in general, not grip, and they come from observational studies. No study read here shows that increasing your grip, on its own, reduces the risk of death.

Do young adults squeeze less hard than before?

The argument “modern life is weakening our hands” rests on little. A 2016 American study measured 237 students aged 20 to 34 and compared them with the 1985 norms.18

Among the 20-24-year-olds in this study, the right hand squeezes less hard than in the 1985 norms

1985 norms2016 study

Means in kg, right hand. In 1985, the norms are based on 29 men and 26 women of this age. The gaps calculated here are 9.2 kg in men and 4.6 kg in women. Source: Fain and Weatherford, Journal of Hand Therapy, 2016, table 1.18

What this means

In this sample, the students squeeze less hard than their elders of 1985. The authors suggest that work has moved away from manual tasks, but their study did not measure the participants' activities: this is a lead, not a result.

The limitations matter. The sample is small, recruited without random selection in a single state, and the authors acknowledge that it may over-represent sedentary people.18 Among children and adolescents aged 9 to 17, an analysis of 2,216,320 young people in 19 countries, between 1967 and 2017, finds a 19.4% rise in grip.19 Among 6,308 Japanese sport students, grip fell in the 1980s-1990s, then stabilised after 2000, with 8.1 kg less in 2016 than at the 1984 peak.20 Three populations, three trajectories: the “silent decline” of young adults is an open question, not an established finding.

The answer to the question

Back to the question: does your grip say anything reliable about your future health, and what can you do with it at your age? Here is the answer, with the degree of certainty for each part.

What is solid. A grip clearly below that of people of your age and sex goes, on average, with a higher risk of death in many countries, and with more difficulty walking and getting up twenty-five years later. This link holds up when age, smoking and known diseases are accounted for.

What is probable. Grip is a proxy for muscular strength and general condition. The link exists from adolescence, which makes it hard to believe that it only involves people who are already ill. Strength training is linked to a lower risk of death and raises grip, even if modestly.

What is not established. That grip causes anything at all: the only clue of causality, genetic, concerns fracture. That training your grip protects. That the test, on its own, is a good tool for individual screening. And that young adults squeeze less hard than before.

At your age, the honest answer is therefore: your number is neither a prediction nor a diagnosis. It is a benchmark for placing yourself, whose value comes from repeating it over time and from what it prompts you to do for your overall strength.

What to put in place

These actions come from what the studies allow us to say. The frequencies suggested are THW suggestions: no study read here sets an interval.

  1. Measure yourself with the protocol on this page, and only that one.Same position, same number of attempts, same hand. The number can only be compared with a norm table measured in the same way: the values from the British study give an order of magnitude, the page's norm table takes precedence.
  2. Place yourself for your age and sex.Benchmarks from the British study for a 30-year-old man: median 51 kg, 10% of men below 38 kg. For a 30-year-old woman: median 31 kg, 10% below 24 kg.2 Being below these thresholds is not a diagnosis, but it is a reason to look at the rest of your strength and, with unusual fatigue or loss of strength, to talk to a doctor.
  3. Add a leg measurement.Grip represents only part of your strength: pair it with a leg test, for example timed chair stands.
  4. Train your overall strength, at least two days a week.This is the WHO recommendation: major muscle groups, with weights or body weight.17 The effect associated with strength training seems maximal at around 30 to 60 minutes per week.16 Including pulling and carrying movements (pull-ups, rows, deadlifts, carries) is a logical choice for grip, not a study result.
  5. Retest, do not optimise.THW suggestion: every three months if you change your training, every six to twelve months otherwise. Compare yourself with your own result. A clear and unexplained drop warrants talking to a doctor. Training solely to push the number up has not been shown to be useful.

This page's test gives the protocol and the norm table to place yourself. It does not replace medical advice.

What these studies do not say
  • These are observational studies. A weak grip may reflect an illness or a frail general condition as much as it may contribute to one.
  • The large cohorts mostly involve middle-aged or older adults. The 16% per 5 kg increment is not a prediction for a 25-year-old.
  • No trial read here shows that increasing your grip reduces the risk of death or loss of independence.
  • The comparison with 1985 rests on small samples from different eras.

Frequently asked questions

My grip is weak. Is that serious?

Not in itself. A single value says nothing about your state of health. Compare it with your age, your sex, and above all your progress over time. The thresholds of 27 kg and 16 kg are used to identify weakness in older people, not to judge a young adult.2

Will squeezing a ball or a gripper make me live longer?

This has not been shown. The large studies show a link, not the effect of targeted training. General strength training, as the WHO recommends, remains a solid foundation.17

Are men and women compared on the same scale?

No. Men are stronger than women from adolescence: at 30, the median is 51 kg against 31 kg.2 Always compare yourself with your own sex.
